          <p class="explanation">Taimur Abdaal leads design at <a href="https://tryretool.com?utm_campaign=css_tricks" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow">Retool</a>, a fast way to build internal tools. They’re working on a new design system for their platform, to let anyone easily build beautiful custom apps. Typography will be a huge part of this and Taimur wrote this based on that experience.</p>
<p>You may have read the title for this post and thought, “Why on earth does a developer need to know anything about typography?” I mean, there’s already a lot on your plate and you’re making hundreds of decisions a day. Should you use React or Vue? npm or Yarn? ES6 or ES7? Sadly, this often leaves something like type as an afterthought. But, let’s remember that <a href="https://ia.net/topics/the-web-is-all-about-typography-period" rel="nofollow noopener">web design is 95% typography</a>:</p>
<blockquote><p>95% of the information on the web is written language. It is only logical to say that a web designer should get good training in the main discipline of shaping written information, in other words: Typography.</p></blockquote>
<p>Even though we deal with content everyday — whether reading, writing, or designing it — typography can be daunting to delve into because it’s filled with jargon and subjectivity, and it’s uncommon to see it taught extensively at school.</p>
<p>This is intended as a practical guide for developers to learn web typography. We’ll cover a range of practical and useful topics, like how to choose and use custom fonts on the web, but more importantly, how to lay text out to create a pleasant user experience. We’ll go over the principles of typography and the CSS properties that control them, as well as handy tips to get good results, quickly.</p>
<p><span id="more-283420"></span></p>
<h3><a href="#what-is-typography" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="what-is-typography"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>What is typography?</h3>
<p>First and foremost, typography is about usability. Type is the <a href="https://ia.net/topics/the-web-is-all-about-typography-period" rel="nofollow noopener">user interface</a> for conveying information, and conveying information is what we’re here to do on the web. There are many levers we can pull to affect the usability of reading text, and only by being deliberate about these can we create a pleasant experience for our users.</p>
<p>After (and <em>only</em> after) usability, typography is about emotion. Do the letters complement your content, or contradict it? Do they amplify your brand’s personality, or dampen it? Applied to the same text, different type will make people feel different things. Being deliberate about typography lets us control these feelings.</p>
<figure id="post-283455" class="align-left media-283455"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/experience.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Same text, different personalities. I’ll bet the first experience is much more expensive. Typefaces: Bodoni 72 (Top), Tsukushi A Round Gothic (Bottom)</figcaption></figure>
<p>Despite what many <a href="https://digitaldeepak.com/golden-ratio-typography/" rel="nofollow noopener">golden ratio enthusiasts</a> might try to tell you, typography isn’t an exact science. Good guidelines will get you most of the way there, but you’ll need to apply a little intuition too. Luckily, you’ve been reading text your whole life — books, magazines, the Internet — so you have a lot more untapped intuition than you think!</p>
<h3><a href="#whats-in-a-font" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="whats-in-a-font"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>What’s in a font?</h3>
<p>Let’s start off by getting a handle on some basic terminology and how fonts are categorized.</p>
<h4><a href="#typeface-vs-font" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="typeface-vs-font"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Typeface vs. Font</h4>
<p>This is how the two have traditionally been defined and distinguished from one another:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Typeface:</strong> The design of a collection of glyphs (e.g. letters, numbers, symbols)</li>
<li><strong>Font:</strong> A specific size, weight, or style of a typeface (e.g. regular, bold, italic)</li>
</ul>
<p>In essence, a typeface is like a song and a font is like its MP3 file. You’ll see both terms used in typography literature, so it’s worth knowing the distinction. “Font vs. Typeface” is also a bit of meme in the design community — you might see it crop up on Twitter, so it’ll help to be “in the know.”</p>

<p>But, more recently, you can essentially use both terms interchangeably and people will know what you mean.</p>
<h4><a href="#how-fonts-are-categorized" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="how-fonts-are-categorized"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>How fonts are categorized</h4>
<p>The broadest split is between <em>serif</em> and <em>sans-serif</em> typefaces. It’s likely you’ve come across these terms just by seeing some typeface names floating around (like, ahem, <em>Comic Sans</em>).</p>
<p>A “serif” is a small stroke attached to the ends of letters, giving them a traditional feel. In fact, most books and newspapers are set in serif typefaces. On the contrary, sans-serif typefaces don’t have these extra strokes, giving them a smooth, modern feel.</p>
<figure id="post-283435" class="align-left media-283435"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/s_FB64E0419C360FFF493C6558F3D017A34BD0F14D3B3A1B417EB66C07CF44FFD2_1548860551288_serifvssans.png?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Times (left) and Helvetica Neue (right)</figcaption></figure>
<p>Both serif and sans-serif have categories within them. For example, serif has sub-categories including <em>didone</em>, <em>slab</em> and <em>old style</em>.</p>
<figure id="post-283450" class="align-left media-283450"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/s_FB64E0419C360FFF493C6558F3D017A34BD0F14D3B3A1B417EB66C07CF44FFD2_1548860611131_serifs.png?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Didot (left), Rockwell (center) and Hoefler Text (right)</figcaption></figure>
<p>As far as sans-serif goes, it includes <em>humanist</em>, <em>geometric</em> and <em>grotesk</em> as sub-categories.</p>
<figure id="post-283436" class="align-left media-283436"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/s_FB64E0419C360FFF493C6558F3D017A34BD0F14D3B3A1B417EB66C07CF44FFD2_1548860620748_sans.png?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Gill Sans (left), Futura (center) and Aktiv Grotesk (right)</figcaption></figure>
<p><em>Monospace</em> fonts (yes, fonts) are a noteworthy category all its own. Each glyph (i.e. letter/number/symbol) in a monospace font has the same width (hence the <em>mono spacing</em> terminology), so it’s possible to arrange them into visual structures. You may be well familiar with monospace because we see it often when writing code, where it’s helpful to make brackets and indents line up visually. The code editor you have open right now is likely using monospace.</p>
<figure id="post-283456" class="align-left media-283456"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/monospace.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Monaco</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a href="#how-to-choose-fonts-and-font-pairings" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="how-to-choose-fonts-and-font-pairings"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>How to choose fonts and font pairings</h3>
<p>This is subjective and depends on what you’re trying to do. Each typeface has its own personality, so you’ll have to find one that aligns with your brand or the content it’s communicating. Typefaces have to be considered within the context that they’re being applied. Are we looking for formality? Maybe start with the serif family. Warm, fun and friendly? That might be a cue for sans-serif. Heck, there’s a time and a place even for Comic Sans… really! Just know that there is no hard science to choosing a font, and even the most trained of typographers are considering contextual cues to find the “right” one.</p>
<p>But fonts can be paired together in the same design. For example, some designs use one typeface for headings and another for body text. This is a good way to get a unique look, but it does take a fair bit of work to get it right. Like colors in a palette, some typefaces work well together while others clash. And even purposeful clashing can make sense, again, given the right context.</p>
<p>The only way to find out if two fonts are complementary is to see them together. Tools like <a href="https://fontpair.co/" rel="nofollow noopener">FontPair</a> and <a href="http://www.typeconnection.com/" rel="nofollow noopener">TypeConnection</a> can help with this. If a font catches your eye when surfing the web, <a href="https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/whatfont/jabopobgcpjmedljpbcaablpmlmfcogm?hl=en" rel="nofollow noopener">WhatFont</a> is a great browser extension to help identify it. Another great resource is <a href="https://typewolf.com" rel="nofollow noopener">Typewolf</a> which allows you to see examples of great web typography, including different font combinations in use:</p>
<figure id="post-283438" class="align-left media-283438"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/typewolf-combinations.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Alice Lee (left), American Documentary (center) and Studio Stereo (right)</figcaption></figure>
<p>While there’s a lot of subjectivity in choosing fonts, there are some objective considerations.</p>
<h4><a href="#font-weight-as-a-consideration" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="font-weight-as-a-consideration"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Font weight as a consideration</h4>
<p>Some font families have a wide range of font weights — Light, Book, Regular, Medium, Semi-Bold, Bold, Black — whereas others just have a couple. </p>
<figure id="post-283457" class="align-left media-283457"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/variants.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Inter UI comes with a fantastic range of weights</figcaption></figure>
<p>If you’re building a complex web app UI, you might need a range of font weights to establish hierarchy in different contexts. For something less complex, say a blog, you’ll likely be fine with just a couple. </p>
<figure id="post-283465" class="align-left media-283465"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/heading-systems-1.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Complex UI hierarchy (left) and Simple blog hierarchy (right)</figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_Fonts/Variable_Fonts_Guide" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow" target="_blank">Variable fonts</a> are an exciting new technology that provide precise control over a font’s characteristics. For font weights, this means there’s no longer limitations to using “Light,” “Regular,” and “Bold,” but really any weight in between. <a href="https://v-fonts.com/" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow" target="_blank">Try some variable fonts out here</a> and <a href="https://css-tricks.com/one-file-many-options-using-variable-fonts-web/">check out Ollie Williams’ post as well</a>.</p>
<p>It’s still early days — there aren’t many variable fonts available right now, and browser support is limited. But definitely a space worth watching!</p>
<h4><a href="#consider-the-legibility-of-a-font" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="consider-the-legibility-of-a-font"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Consider the legibility of a font</h4>
<p>Some typefaces are harder to read than others. Stay away from elaborate fonts when it comes to paragraphs, and if you <em>must</em> have tiny text somewhere, make sure its typeface is legible at those tiny sizes.</p>
<p>Of these two examples, which is easier on the eyes? (There is a right answer here. 🙂)</p>

<h4><a href="#remember-fonts-come-in-a-variety-of-styles" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="remember-fonts-come-in-a-variety-of-styles"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Remember, fonts come in a variety of styles</h4>
<p>Making a font bold isn’t as simple as adding an outline to the text, and italics are more than slanted letters. Good fonts have specific bold and italic styles, without which the browser tries to “fake” it:</p>
<figure id="post-283463" class="align-left media-283463"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/faux-true.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Lato</figcaption></figure>
<p>These faux styles tend to reduce legibility and break the text’s visual cohesion because the browser can only do so much with what it’s given. <a href="https://alistapart.com/article/say-no-to-faux-bold" rel="nofollow noopener">Stick to fonts</a> <a href="https://alistapart.com/article/say-no-to-faux-bold" rel="nofollow noopener">that offer</a> <a href="https://alistapart.com/article/say-no-to-faux-bold" rel="nofollow noopener">true bold/italics styles</a>, if you can. </p>
<h4><a href="#other-things-worth-consideration" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="other-things-worth-consideration"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Other things worth consideration</h4>
<p>What we’ve looked at so far are the high-level characteristics and features of fonts that can help us decide which to choose for a particular design or context. There are many other things that can (and probably should) be taken into consideration, including:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Language support:</strong> Some fonts have glyphs for foreign characters, which may be a requirement for a project geared toward a multilingual audience or that contains multilingual content.</li>
<li><strong><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/font-variant-ligatures" rel="nofollow noopener">Ligatures</a>:</strong> Some fonts (typically serifs) have glyphs to replace otherwise awkward characters, like ﬃ and ﬄ which are multiple characters in a single glyph.</li>
<li><strong>File size:</strong> You’re a developer, so I know you care about performance. Some fonts come in bigger files than others and those can cause a site to take a hit on load times.</li>
</ul>
<h3><a href="#using-fonts-on-the-world-wide-web" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="using-fonts-on-the-world-wide-web"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Using fonts on the world wide web</h3>
<p>A mere 10 years ago, there were two complex ways to use custom fonts on the web:</p>
<ul>
<li>SiFR: Embedding a Flash (remember that thing?) widget to render text.</li>
<li>cufon: converting the font to a proprietary format, and using a specific JavaScript rendering engine to generate the text using VML on an HTML <code><canvas></code>.</li>
</ul>
<p>Today, there’s all we need is a single simple one: <code>@font-face</code>. It lets you specify a font file URL, which the browser then downloads and uses on your site. </p>
<p>You can use the <code>@font-face</code> declaration to define your custom font:</p>
<pre rel="CSS"><code class="language-css">@font-face {
  font-family: 'MyWebFont';
  src: url('webfont.eot'); /* IE9 Compat Modes */
  src: url('webfont.eot?#iefix') format('embedded-opentype'), /* IE6-IE8 */
        url('webfont.woff2') format('woff2'), /* Super Modern Browsers */
        url('webfont.woff') format('woff'), /* Pretty Modern Browsers */
        url('webfont.ttf')  format('truetype'), /* Safari, Android, iOS */
        url('webfont.svg#svgFontName') format('svg'); /* Legacy iOS */
}</code></pre>
<p>And then refer to it as normal, by the <code>font-family</code> attribute:</p>
<pre rel="CSS"><code class="language-css">body {
  font-family: 'MyWebFont', Fallback, sans-serif;
}</code></pre>
<p class="explanation">Even though <code>@font-face</code> is light years ahead of the old school approaches to custom web fonts, there is quite a bit to consider as far as browser support goes. Here’s a guide to getting the <a href="https://css-tricks.com/snippets/css/using-font-face/) for loading fonts">right amount of cross-browser support</a>.</p>
<h4><a href="#the-impact-of-fonts-on-performance" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="the-impact-of-fonts-on-performance"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>The impact of fonts on performance</h4>
<p>Performance is the only downside to using custom fonts on the web. Fonts are relatively large assets — often hundreds of kilobytes in size — and will have and adverse effect on the speed of any site.</p>
<p>Here are some tips to soften the blow:</p>
<ul>
<li>Use <a href="https://gzip.org/" rel="nofollow noopener">GZIP compression</a> on your web font files.</li>
<li>Disable font features you don’t need, e.g. <a href="https://www.typotheque.com/articles/hinting" rel="nofollow noopener">hinting</a>, <a href="https://type.method.ac/" rel="nofollow noopener">kerning.</a></li>
<li>Remove glyphs that you don’t need, e.g. foreign language characters.</li>
</ul>
<p>One tool that can help tailor a font file to suit your needs is <a href="https://transfonter.org/" rel="nofollow noopener">Transfonter</a>. Just make sure you have the rights to any font that you want to use on your site because, well, it’s just the right thing to do.</p>
<h4><a href="#some-services-will-host-web-fonts-for-you" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="some-services-will-host-web-fonts-for-you"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Some services will host web fonts for you</h4>
<p>One other significant way to shed some of the weight of using custom web fonts is to use a service that will host and serve them for you. The benefit here is that third-parties store the files on a speedy <a href="https://css-tricks.com/adding-a-cdn-to-your-website/">CDN</a>, optimize them, and serve them to your site via a JavaScript snippet that gets dropped into the document head. In short: it takes a lot of hassle off your hands. </p>
<p>How easy is it to use a hosted service? Consider that using anything on Google Fonts only requires a single <code><link></code> in the HTML head:</p>
<pre rel="HTML"><code class="language-html"><html>
  <head>
    <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Roboto" rel="stylesheet">
  <style>
    body {
      font-family: 'Roboto', sans-serif;
    }
  </style>
</head>

<!-- Rest of the document --></code></pre>
<p>This example was taken from <a href="https://fonts.google.com/" rel="nofollow noopener">Google Fonts</a> — the most popular hosted font service. It’s free to use, and, at the time of writing, has a catalog of 915 font families. The quality of these can be hit-or-miss. Some are truly top-notch — beautiful design, many weights, true bold/italics, and advanced features like ligatures. Others, typically the more novel designs, are bare-bones, and might not be suitable for serious projects with evolving needs.</p>
<p><a href="https://fonts.adobe.com/" rel="nofollow noopener">Adobe Fonts</a> is also very popular. It comes bundled with Adobe’s Creative Cloud offering, which starts at $20.99 per month. At the time of writing, it has a catalog of 1,636 font families. These are typically high-quality fonts that you’d have to pay for, but with Adobe Fonts, you can access them all in a Netflix all-you-can-eat model. </p>
<p>Here are some other options:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://edgewebfonts.adobe.com/index" rel="nofollow noopener"><strong>Adobe Edge Web Fonts</strong></a>: This is the free version of Adobe Fonts. Adobe partnered with Google on this, so there’s a lot of overlap with the Google Fonts library. It has 503 font families in total.</li>
<li><a href="https://fontspring.com" rel="nofollow noopener"><strong>Fontspring</strong></a>: This is a massive library of over 14,000 font families, but with an individual licensing model. This means paying more up-front, starting at ~$20 per individual font (and per weight or style), but no recurring costs. It’s also self-serve — you’ll have to host the files yourself.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.myfonts.com" rel="nofollow noopener"><strong>MyFonts by Monotype</strong></a>: This is major type foundry. Similar to Fontspring: massive library of font families with an individual licensing model.</li>
<li><a href="https://fonts.com" rel="nofollow noopener"><strong>Fonts.com</strong></a>: This is similar to Fontspring. Options for one-off or pay-as-you go pricing (based on page views).
<li><a href="https://www.typography.com/webfonts/" rel="nofollow noopener"><strong>Cloud.typography by Hoefler&Co</strong></a>: This is a major type foundry. Over 1,000 font families (all by Hoefler&Co), with options for hosted (subscription, starting at $99 per year) or self-hosted (individually licensed) web fonts. The benefit here is that you get access to a library of fonts you cannot find anywhere else.</li>
<li><a href="https://fontstand.com/" rel="nofollow noopener"><strong>Fontstand</strong></a>: This services allows you to “rent” individual fonts cheaply on a monthly basis, starting ~$10 per month), which you get to own automatically after 12 months. To date, it boasts 1,500 families, with a hosted web font service.</li>
</ul>
<h3><a href="#css-and-typography" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="css-and-typography"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>CSS and Typography</h3>
<p>OK, let’s move on to the intersection of design and development. We’ve covered a lot of the foundational terms and concepts of typography, but now we can turn our attention to what affordances we have to manipulate and style type, specifically with CSS.</p>
<h4><a href="#adjusting-font-sizing" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="adjusting-font-sizing"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Adjusting font sizing</h4>
<p>Changing the size of a font is something that inevitably pops up in a typical project. Size is important because it creates hierarchy, implicitly guiding the user through the page. So, in this section, we’re going to look at two CSS features that are available in our tool belt for adjusting font sizes to create better content hierarchy.</p>
<h5><a href="#sizes-can-be-expressed-in-a-different-units-of-measure" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="sizes-can-be-expressed-in-a-different-units-of-measure"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Sizes can be expressed in a different units of measure</h5>
<p>Did you know that there are 15 different units for sizing in CSS? Crazy, right? Most of us are probably aware of and comfortable working with pixels (<code>px</code>) but there are so many other ways we can define the size of a font.</p>
<p>Some of these are <em>relative</em> units, and others are <em>absolute</em>. The actual size of an element expressed in relative units depends on other parts of the page, while the actual size of an element expressed in absolute units is always the same. And, as you might expect, that difference is important because they serve different functions, depending on a design’s needs.</p>
<p>Of the 15 units we have available, we will selectively look at two in particular: <code>px</code> and <code>em</code>. Not only are these perhaps the two most used units that you’ll see used to define font sizes, but they also perfectly demonstrate the difference between absolute and relative sizing.</p>
<p>First off, <code>px</code> is an absolute unit and it actually doesn’t have much to do with pixels (it’s considered an <a href="http://inamidst.com/stuff/notes/csspx" rel="nofollow noopener">angular measurement</a>), but it’s defined so that a line of width <code>1px</code> appears sharp and visible, no matter the screen resolution. The <code>px</code> value corresponds, roughly, to a little more than the distance from the highest ascender (e.g. the top of the letter A) to the lowest descender (e.g. the bottom of the letter p) in the font. Some fonts have taller letters than others, so <code>16px</code> in one font might look noticeably “bigger” than <code>16px</code> in another. Yet another consideration to take into account when choosing a font!</p>
<p>Interestingly enough, when it comes to typography, the <code>px</code> is a unit to be understood, but not used. The true purpose of <code>px</code> units is to serve as the foundation of a type system based on relative units. In other words, it’s an absolute value that a relative unit can point to in order to define its own size relative to that value.</p>
<p>Which takes us to <code>em</code>, a relative unit. Text with a font size of <code>2em</code> would be twice as big as the <code>font-size</code> of its parent element. Each device has its own default <code>font-size</code> for the <code>body</code> element. For example, desktop browsers usually default to <code>16px</code>. Other devices (e.g. mobile phones and TVs) might have different defaults that are optimized for their form factors.</p>
<p>The <code>em</code> lets you reason about your typography intuitively: “I want this title to be twice as big as the paragraph text” corresponds directly to <code>2em</code>. It’s also easy to maintain — if you need a media query to make everything bigger on mobile, it’s a simple matter of increasing one <code>font-size</code> attribute. Dealing in <code>em</code> units also lets you set other typographical elements in relation to <code>font-size</code>, as we’ll see later.</p>
<h5><a href="#there-are-semantic-html-elements-that-css-can-target-to-adjust-size" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="there-are-semantic-html-elements-that-css-can-target-to-adjust-size"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>There are semantic HTML elements that CSS can target to adjust size</h5>
<p>You’re sold on the <code>em</code>, but how many <code>em</code> units should each element be? You’ll want to have a range of text sizes to establish hierarchy between different elements of your page. More often than not, you’ll see hierarchies that are six level deep, which corresponds to the HTML heading elements, <code>h1</code> through <code>h6</code>.</p>
<p>The right size scale depends on the use case. As a guideline, many people choose to use a <em>modular scale</em>. That refers to a scale based on a constant ratio for successive text elements in the hierarchy.</p>
<figure id="post-283442" class="align-left media-283442"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/s_FB64E0419C360FFF493C6558F3D017A34BD0F14D3B3A1B417EB66C07CF44FFD2_1548871340137_modularscale.png?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Example of a modular scale with a ratio of 1.4</figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="https://www.modularscale.com/" rel="nofollow noopener">Modular Scales</a> is a tool by Tim Brown, who popularized this approach, which makes it easy to visualize different size scales.</p>
<h4><a href="#adjusting-a-fonts-vertical-spacing-and-alignment" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="adjusting-a-fonts-vertical-spacing-and-alignment"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Adjusting a font’s vertical spacing and alignment</h4>
<p>The physical size of a font is a super common way we use CSS to style a font, but vertical spacing is another incredibly powerful way CSS can help improve the legibility of content.</p>
<h5><a href="#use-line-height-to-define-how-tall-to-make-a-line-of-text" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="use-line-height-to-define-how-tall-to-make-a-line-of-text"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Use line-height to define how tall to make a line of text</h5>
<p>Line height is one of the most important factors affecting readability. It’s controlled by the <code>line-height</code> property, best expressed as a unit-less number that corresponds to a multiple of the defined font size.</p>
<p>Let’s say we are working with a computed font size of <code>16px</code> (specified in the CSS as <code>em</code> units, of course), a <code>line-height</code> of <code>1.2</code> would make each line <code>19.2px</code> tall. (Remember that <code>px</code>  aren’t actually pixels, so decimals are valid!)</p>
<p>Most browsers default to a <code>line-height</code>  of <code>1.2</code> but the problem is that this is usually too tight — you probably want something closer to <code>1.5</code> because provides a little more breathing room for your eyes when reading.</p>
<p>Here are some general guidelines to define a good line-height:</p>
<ul>
<li>Increase <code>line-height</code> for thick fonts</li>
<li>Increase <code>line-height</code> when fonts are a dark color</li>
<li>Increase <code>line-height</code> for long-form content</li>
</ul>
<figure id="post-283458" class="align-left media-283458"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/line-height.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Increasing the line-height can drastically improve legibility</figcaption></figure>
<h5><a href="#fonts-cant-dance-but-they-still-have-rhythm" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="fonts-cant-dance-but-they-still-have-rhythm"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Fonts can’t dance, but they still have rhythm</h5>
<p>Rhythm describes how text flows vertically on a page. Much like music, some amount of consistency and structure usually leads to good “rhythm.” Like most design techniques, rhythm isn’t an exact science but there are some sensible guidelines that give good results.</p>
<p>One school of thought prescribes the use of paragraph line height as a baseline unit from which all other spacing is derived. This includes gaps between paragraphs and headings and padding between the text and other page elements. </p>
<p>Under this system, you might set the line height of a heading to twice the line height of paragraphs, and leave a one-line gap between a heading and paragraph. Handily, you can use the same <code>em</code> units to define margins and padding, so there’s really no need to hard-code anything.</p>
<figure id="post-283598" class="align-left media-283598"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/vertical-rhythm.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /></figure>
<p><a href="https://betterwebtype.com/rhythm-in-web-typography" rel="nofollow noopener">Read more about rhythm here.</a></p>
<h4><a href="#horizontal-shape" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="horizontal-shape"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>Horizontal Shape</h4>
<p>Hopefully, you’re convinced by now that vertical spacing is an important factor in improving legibility that we can control in CSS. Equally important is the horizontal spacing of individual characters and the overall width of content.</p>
<h5><a href="#css-can-control-the-space-between-letters" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="css-can-control-the-space-between-letters"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>CSS can control the space between letters</h5>
<p>Letter spacing is one of the most important factors affecting legibility. It is controlled by the CSS <code>letter-spacing</code> property, best expressed (again) in <code>em</code> units to keep everything relative. Tracking (the typography term for “letter spacing”) depends entirely on the font — some fonts will look great by default, while others might need a little tweaking.</p>
<p>In general, you only need to worry about letter spacing for text elements that are particularly big or small because most fonts are spaced well at a typical paragraph size. </p>
<p>For larger text, like headings and titles, you’ll often want to reduce the space between letters. And a little bit of space goes a long way. For example, <code>-0.02em</code> is a tiny decimal, but a good starting point, which can be tweaked until it looks just right to your eye. The only time you should think about increasing letter spacing is when dealing with stylistically unusual text — things like all-capped titles and even some number sequences.</p>
<figure id="post-283459" class="align-left media-283459"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/letter-spacing.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /><figcaption>Adding or subtracting as little as 0.02em can refine the appearance of words</figcaption></figure>
<p>Some specific pairs of letters, like <code>AV</code>, can look awkwardly spaced without a little manual tweaking. Well-crafted fonts typically specify custom spacing for such pairs, and setting the <code>font-kerning</code> property to <code>normal</code> lets you enable this. Browsers disable this on smaller text by default. Here is a little <a href="https://css-tricks.com/methods-controlling-spacing-web-typography/">more on letter spacing</a>, as well as other CSS tools we have to control font spacing in general.</p>
<h5><a href="#the-length-of-a-line-of-text-is-more-important-than-you-might-think" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="the-length-of-a-line-of-text-is-more-important-than-you-might-think"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>The length of a line of text is more important than you might think</h5>
<p>It’s unpleasant for our eyes to move long distances while reading, so the width of lines should be deliberate. The general consensus is that a good width is somewhere between 60 and 70 characters per line. If you find that a line of text (especially for long-form content) drastically falls outside this range, then start adjusting.</p>
<p>The <code>ch</code> is a little-known CSS unit that we didn’t cover earlier, but can be helpful to keep line length in check. It’s a relative unit, defined as the width of the <code>0</code> character in the element’s font. Because narrow characters like <code>l</code> and <code>i</code> are relatively frequent, setting the width of a text container to something like <code>50ch</code> should result in lines that are 60-70 character long.</p>
<pre rel="CSS"><code class="language-css">p {
  width: 50ch;
}</code></pre>
<figure id="post-283461" class="align-left media-283461"><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" src="https://i0.wp.com/css-tricks.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/characters-per-line.jpg?ssl=1" alt="" /></figure>
<h4><a href="#css-can-smooth-otherwise-crispy-fonts" aria-hidden="true" class="aal_anchor" id="css-can-smooth-otherwise-crispy-fonts"><svg aria-hidden="true" class="aal_svg" height="16" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="16"><path fill-rule="evenodd" d="M4 9h1v1H4c-1.5 0-3-1.69-3-3.5S2.55 3 4 3h4c1.45 0 3 1.69 3 3.5 0 1.41-.91 2.72-2 3.25V8.59c.58-.45 1-1.27 1-2.09C10 5.22 8.98 4 8 4H4c-.98 0-2 1.22-2 2.5S3 9 4 9zm9-3h-1v1h1c1 0 2 1.22 2 2.5S13.98 12 13 12H9c-.98 0-2-1.22-2-2.5 0-.83.42-1.64 1-2.09V6.25c-1.09.53-2 1.84-2 3.25C6 11.31 7.55 13 9 13h4c1.45 0 3-1.69 3-3.5S14.5 6 13 6z"></path></svg></a>CSS can smooth otherwise crispy fonts</h4>
<p><code>-webkit-font-smoothing</code> is a nifty CSS property that controls how fonts are anti-aliased. This is a fancy way of saying it can draw shades of gray around otherwise square pixels to create a smoother appearance. Do note, however, the <code>-webkit</code> prefix there, because that indicates that the property is only supported by WebKit browsers, e.g. Safari.</p>
<p>The default setting is <code>subpixel-antialiased</code>, but it’s worth seeing what your type looks like when it’s set to just <code>antialiased</code>. It can improve the way many fonts look, especially for text on non-white backgrounds. </p>
<p>At small font sizes, this should be used with caution — it lowers contrast, affecting readability. You should also make sure to adjust <code>letter-spacing</code> when using this, since greater anti-aliasing will increase the space between letters.</p>
